title: Slope Is Not Height
subtitle: The y-value shows position. The slope shows velocity.
visualLead: Move along the graph; compare position with slope.
focus: The amber point rises with time, but the line's teal slope stays at 3 m/s.
idea: On a position–time graph, vertical height is position, while slope is change in position divided by change in time. They describe different quantities and have different units.

challenge.prompt: At t = 2 s, the position graph x(t) = 2 + 3t has height 8 m. What is the object's velocity?
choices: 8 m/s, because the graph has height 8.
feedback: Correct. A linear position graph has constant velocity equal to its slope.
Time is the horizontal coordinate, not the velocity.

title: Can Negative Acceleration Speed You Up?
subtitle: Direction matters more than the sign alone.
visualLead: Choose the directions of velocity and acceleration.
focus: If velocity and acceleration point the same way, the object's speed increases.
idea: Speed is the magnitude of velocity. Negative acceleration means a change toward the negative direction—not necessarily slowing down. For nonzero velocity, acceleration in the same direction makes the speed grow.

challenge.prompt: A cart is moving left and also accelerates left. What happens to its speed?
choices: Its speed decreases because acceleration is negative.
Its speed stays unchanged because the arrows cancel.
feedback: Correct. Velocity becomes more negative and its magnitude increases.
Negative acceleration describes direction on a chosen axis, not automatically slowing down.
Velocity and acceleration have different units and do not cancel as forces.

title: The Limit Is Not the Point
subtitle: Change f(1) without changing the limit.
visualLead: Change the function value at x = 1. Watch the open circle.
focus: The teal curve still approaches 2 from both sides—even if the filled dot moves.
idea: A limit is about values of f(x) near the target. Changing the value at that one input leaves the nearby graph unchanged. Thus f(1) and limₓ→1 f(x) can be different.

challenge.prompt: Suppose limₓ→1 f(x) = 2 but f(1) = 5. Which statement is correct?
choices: The limit remains 2; the function value at 1 is 5.
The limit does not exist because the function has a value.
feedback: Changing a single function value does not change the approach from nearby x-values.
Correct. The limit and the actual point value can differ.
A defined value at the point does not prevent a two-sided limit.
